extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students studying patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Determining what kinds of things are proper subjects of a patent (principles, processes, manufactures, applications, combinations) and how to test claims for being patentable and for infringement. Covers doctrine distinguishing abstract discoveries from embodied applications, examples, and tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: No patent for a mere principle or abstract science
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent cannot be for a mere elementary principle, intellectual discovery, science, or an effect; principles are elements of science and not themselves patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a 'principle constitutes an important part of the discovery it must be a principle put in practice and applied to some art.' The textbook repeats that an abstract art or principle (e.g., a newly-discovered principle in science) cannot be the subject of a patent because it would monopolize every object to which the principle could be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent must be for a mode/means of producing an effect (not for the effect alone)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must be for the mode or means by which an effect is produced rather than for the abstract effect itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim must specify the manner of producing the effect (the mode, method, or apparatus). The book notes 'there cannot be a patent for an effect, but it must be for the mode or means by which the effect is produced.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture/process/method/practical application are patentable subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory generic term 'manufacture' was construed broadly to include processes, methods, and practical applications of principles (e.g., Watt's case—mode of lessening steam consumption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus patents may be taken for processes or practical applications of principles provided there is an invented mode of carrying the principle into effect and the invention produces a vendible, practical result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodiment requirement — principle must be embodied so it can act
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle, when embodied so as to be capable of being made active and to produce an effect, may be the subject-matter of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once embodied, others putting that principle into use in another form raises a jury question whether that form is a substantial adaptation of the principle applied to the same end. Examples: implementations of heating air, welding tubes, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invented mode requirement to secure broad protection
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim protection against other means of carrying the same principle into effect, the patentee must have invented some mode of carrying the principle into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patentee has not invented any mode of carrying the principle into effect, he cannot claim a monopoly over all modes (Jupe v. Pratt). But if he did invent a mode, he may be entitled to protection from 'all other modes of carrying the same principle into effect,' treated as piracy by imitating that original invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims cannot be unrealistically broad (no claim to an art in the abstract or all means)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that purports to cover an art or method in the abstract or 'by any means' is invalid; patents must be limited to particular methods or machinery described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wyeth v. Stone: claim to 'cut ice ... by means of any other power than human' was 'unmaintainable.' A timely disclaimer narrowing the claim to particular methods can sometimes save a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against colorable variations — substantial equivalence test
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who invented a mode of carrying a principle into effect may be protected against 'colorable variations' that in substance carry the same principle into effect to obtain the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination is fact-specific (jury): whether defendant's form is merely a colorable variation of the patentee's mode. Courts look to whether variations are merely in form while answering the same end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of a known agent/thing to a particular effect can be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a known substance, agent, or thing in a new way to produce a given effect may constitute patentable subject-matter (even if the agent itself was known).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Daniell's immersion of cloth in hot water; Hall's application of gas flame to singe fibres — the novelty was in the application, not in the agent. The book emphasizes application/adaptation of known things to new purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations of known elements may be patentable if they produce a new/better/cheaper article
rubrics_metrics.description: A new combination of materials or known means may be patentable where the combination produces a new article, or a better or cheaper article to the public than previously produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: combination of hot blast with anthracite coal in ironmaking — if the result is improved, the combination may be 'an invention or manufacture intended by the statute.' The specification must clearly express that it is the new combination or application being claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must clearly express the claimed new combination or application
rubrics_metrics.description: When the invention is a combination or an application of known agents, the specification must clearly state that the claim is in respect of that new combination or application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to clearly express the combination or to disclaim separately claimed parts can lead to invalidity; courts examine whether the specification limits the monopoly to the inventive combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in ingredients or order of process steps can be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitting an ingredient previously thought essential, or changing the order of process steps using the same solutions, may constitute a new invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a patent for making double canvass without starch; rendering fabrics water-proof by immersing in solutions in a different order — these procedural changes altered the series of processes and were treated as patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two broad classes of patentable inventions (application vs discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are (1) inventions that are new applications of known agents/things leading to a change in processes or results, and (2) discoveries and applications of new agents/things producing new effects or results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book suggests avoiding rigid classification; instead test each case by general principles, but recognizes these two helpful categories (e.g., electric telegraph, photography depending on view of agent/result).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part test for analyzing application of a principle
rubrics_metrics.description: To analyze whether an application of a principle is patentable: (1) Are the agents employed newly discovered or well known? (2) Are they applied in a new method? (3) Do they produce, as applied, a new or an old result?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this analysis to determine patentable character; each factor influences whether the subject-matter is eligible — the conclusion depends on the particular facts of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: When invention lies in conception rather than machinery, machinery is incidental
rubrics_metrics.description: If the most important part of an invention is the original idea (conception) rather than the particular means, the principle carried into practice by some means constitutes the subject-matter; the machinery used is incidental, not of the essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases, imitating the character/idea may be piracy even if the infringer uses different means — courts consider whether the essence of the invention has been taken.
